read.sections.0.text.back: Borobudur is a Buddhist temple in Central Java, Indonesia. This temple was built in the 700s and 800s. This temple has stone terraces, walls carved with pictures, and 72 small stupas, or bell-shaped towers. Each stupa contains a statue of the Buddha. UNESCO explains that its levels follow an idea about the universe in Buddhist teaching. Centuries later, people faced a new question: how should this temple be conserved? A large restoration took place from 1973 to 1983. Indonesia and UNESCO did that work, with help from other countries. The people who restored Borobudur did not build it. It helps if we keep these two times apart.
read.sections.0.text.source: Borobudur is a Buddhist monument in Central Java, Indonesia. It was built in the 700s and 800s. It has stone terraces, walls carved with pictures, and 72 small stupas, or bell-shaped towers. Each stupa holds a statue of the Buddha. UNESCO explains that its levels follow a Buddhist idea of the universe. Many centuries later, people faced a new question: how should it be conserved? A large restoration ran from 1973 to 1983. Indonesia and UNESCO did the work, with help from other countries. The people who restored Borobudur did not build it. It helps to keep these two times apart.

read.sections.0.simpler.back: Borobudur is a Buddhist temple on the island of Java. People built it more than 1,000 years ago. This temple has stone steps and walls with carved pictures. At its top there are 72 small stone towers. Each tower contains a statue of the Buddha. From 1973 to 1983, a big team repaired it. This careful work is called conservation. Indonesia and UNESCO did it together. That team did not build that temple.
read.sections.0.simpler.source: Borobudur is a Buddhist temple on the island of Java. People built it more than 1,000 years ago. It has stone steps and walls with carved pictures. At the top are 72 small stone towers. Each one holds a statue of the Buddha. From 1973 to 1983, a big team fixed it. This careful work is called conservation. Indonesia and UNESCO did it together. The team did not build the temple.

read.sections.1.text.note: "As-built drawing" is kept as "gambar as-built", the term used in Indonesian building work, and explained in the next sentence and the glossary. Reviewers: "gambar terbangun" or another everyday phrase may be clearer for learners.
read.sections.1.text.back: An archive is a collection of records kept so that people can study them later. During the restoration, that team took photos, made drawings and films, and wrote reports. An office at Borobudur keeps them until now. Its list counts 71,851 sheets of photos and 6,043 sheets of as-built drawings and maps. An as-built drawing shows what the workers found and recorded while the work went on. That drawing is not a plan from the first builders. A conservator at a later time can compare a photo with a drawing and ask why a repair was made. In 2017, UNESCO gave recognition to that archive. That date is about its records, not about the temple.

read.sections.2.text.back: The second picture is a photo taken in 1976 by Gerard Bolla for UNESCO. That photo records one moment of modern conservation work. Look at what is in the photo, then ask what is outside it. A photo cannot tell us what the first builders planned, or why each repair was chosen. That photo cannot tell us what Borobudur means to every visitor and worshipper. People can add to that record. In 2019, an exhibition of photos by Suparno opened near Borobudur. He worked at the Borobudur office and was trained to photograph the repair work. His memories can answer questions that one photo leaves unanswered.

sensitiveNotes.0.note: "Never rank beliefs" became "jangan pernah membanding-bandingkan keyakinan" (never compare beliefs against each other); "keyakinan" as in KEY_TERMS for Lesson 4.
sensitiveNotes.0.back: Borobudur is a place of worship and pilgrimage for Buddhists until now. Use respectful and neutral words ("Many Buddhists ...", "UNESCO explains ..."), never compare beliefs, and never ask learners about their own religion; in the Speak step, "people who come to worship" is a group to think about, not a question about anyone in the room. Watch the video first: according to UNESCO's record, its narration mentions a volcano and describes a carving of the Buddha being tempted.
sensitiveNotes.0.source: Borobudur is a Buddhist place of worship and pilgrimage today. Use respectful, neutral words ("Many Buddhists ...", "UNESCO explains ..."), never rank beliefs, and never ask learners about their own religion; in Speak, "people who come to worship" is a group to think about, not a question about anyone in the room. Preview the video: by UNESCO's account its narration mentions a volcano and describes a carving of the Buddha being tempted.

educatorNotes.0.back: Aim: learners keep apart the ancient temple (built in the 700s–800s), the 1973–1983 restoration, and the 2017 Memory of the World recognition, then write an accurate, dated photo caption with its two limits. Step for reading evidence: write the three dates in three boxes on the board before learners look at the 1976 photo. A good answer names who (Gerard Bolla for UNESCO), when (1976) and what (modern conservation work), then two questions that photo cannot answer.
educatorNotes.0.source: Aim: learners keep the ancient monument (built 700s–800s), the 1973–1983 restoration and the 2017 Memory of the World recognition apart, and write an accurate, dated caption with two limits. educatorNotes.1.back: Misunderstanding to straighten out: that a conservation photo is evidence about the building of the temple in ancient times. Notes on the sources: the archive's numbers (71,851 photo sheets, 6,043 as-built drawing sheets, 425 project documents) come from Indonesia's nomination form on UNESCO's site; the 2017 date comes from news about that recognition, because UNESCO's own archive page could not be opened. UNESCO's listing says the temple was rebuilt in two stages in the 1900s, the second from 1973 to 1983; this lesson only covers the second stage. The back of the 1976 photo print (Commons file "PHOTO0000003469 0000") carries UNESCO's own typed caption from that time, which is also a source: that caption calls the work "in progress" (going on) and dates UNESCO's agreement with Indonesia to 12 October 1972. Suparno's 2019 exhibition (Borobudur Conservation Office together with UNESCO Jakarta) was reported by The Jakarta Post.

UNESCO's listing says the temple was rebuilt in two phases in the 1900s, the second from 1973 to 1983; the lesson covers only the second.
